newsitem.title: USA: Empire State gunman's letter reveals intended targets.
newsitem.headline: Empire State gunman's letter reveals intended targets.

text.p: The Palestinian gunman who killed one man in a deadly assault at the Empire State Building was targeting Americans, the British and French as enemies of his countrymen and aimed "to murder as many of them as possible," according to a letter he wrote which was released on Tuesday.

Ali Abu Kamal decided to "strike at their own den in New York" and selected the world-famous landmark as the scene of his revenge, according to a letter he carried in a pouch around his neck. Police released copies of the letter at a news conference at City Hall.

Kamal opened fire with a .380-calibre Beretta semiautomatic handgun at dusk on Sunday on the 86th-floor observation deck of the Empire State Building, killing Danish rock musician Christoffer Burmeister and wounding six other people before fatally shooting himself in the head.
His letter blamed Americans, Britons and the French -- all of whom he called his "first enemy" -- as responsible for making the Palestinian people homeless.
"They must be annihilated and exterminated," he wrote, adding that "the Zionists are the paw that carried out their savage aggression."
The letter made no mention of the financial troubles cited by Kamal's family, who said he was upset over allegedly being swindled out of hundreds of thousands of dollars in savings.
In fact, Police Commisioner Howard Safir said there was no evidence Kamal ever had any such money. But he said police still believe Kamal acted alone and had no links to political groups.

The letter, which reads like a hit list of people Kamal held a grudge against, cites a "gang of rogues" whom the retired college professor said attacked him for refusing to help them cheat on an exam.
He also listed an Egyptian police officer he said insulted and beat him in Cairo in the early 1980s, and complained about three students he said once beat and blackmailed his son.

Kamal concluded with an explanation that he would have carried out the shooting much earlier but was tied up with obligations toward his late parents, his brother and sister and his children. The two-page letter was dated Jan. 1, 1996.
"The letter indicates a man who had many, many objects of his hatred, not just one," said Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who said it would take a team of psychiatrists to understand Kamal's motives.
Meanwhile, the 86th-floor observation deck, a popular tourist destination, re-opened to the public for the first time since the tragedy, with heavy new security measures.

Hundreds of visitors, many of whom said they were neither deterred nor frightened in the wake of the shooting, waited in long lines to pass through newly installed metal detectors. The crowd included the usual mix of tour groups and schoolchildren.
The extra security added "just a few minutes" to the waiting time to get to the observation deck, a trek generally slowed by waits for the elevators, a spokesman said.
Kamal's victims remained hospitalized. Rock musician Matthew Gross, 29, of New Jersey, who suffered a gunshot wound to the head, was in critical condition at Bellevue Hospital.

He underwent surgery to relieve swelling of his brain, his second operation since the shooting, a spokeswoman said. Gross played in a band called the Bush Pilots with Burmeister, a 27-year-old guitarist.

Mario Carmona, 51, of Argentina, shot in the neck, and Jacob Schaad, 30, of Switzerland, shot in the chest, were both in stable condition, the hospital said. Also in stable condition at St. Vincent's Hospital were a couple from Verdun, France, and a 35-year-old Bronx man.

In the aftermath of the shooting, New York politicians including Giuliani, Gov. George Pataki, Representative Charles Schumer and Representative Carolyn McCarthy stepped up calls for gun control which they said might have stopped Kamal.
Kamal, who arrived in the United States on Dec. 24, bought the gun in Florida after he obtained a state identification card by checking into a motel in Melbourne, officials said.
